questions.question: Battle of the Sexes is a two-player coordination game in which matching is good for both, but the two ways of matching split the gains differently. Which economic situation has this structure?
options: Two firms set prices; each gains by undercutting whatever the other does
Two firms pick standards; each wants to use a different standard from the rival
Two firms pick a standard; any match beats a mismatch, and both prefer the same one
Two firms pick a common standard; matching helps both, and each prefers its own

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes, each player chooses $O$ or $F$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$. What does iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (deleting strategies that another strategy beats against every opponent strategy) remove?
options: Nothing, because each action is the best reply to the same action
Player 1's $F$ and player 2's $O$, the options each player likes less
Player 2's $O$ first, after which player 1's $F$ becomes dominated
The two mismatched profiles, since they give each player only $0$

questions.question: Battle of the Sexes has two pure Nash equilibria, $(O,O)$, preferred by player 1, and $(F,F)$, preferred by player 2. What can make both players expect the same one of them?
options: Common knowledge that both players are rational payoff maximizers
Each player choosing her own favourite, since both know the other is rational
A convention or pre-play talk that tells both which match to expect
Deleting strictly dominated strategies until a single profile remains

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes, each player chooses $O$ or $F$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$. Player 1 is sure that player 2 will choose $F$, while player 2 is sure that player 1 will choose $O$, and each plays a best response to her own belief. Which profile and payoffs result?
options: $(O,F)$, with payoffs $(0,0)$
$(O,O)$, with payoffs $(2,1)$
$(F,F)$, with payoffs $(1,2)$
$(F,O)$, with payoffs $(0,0)$

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes, each player chooses $O$ or $F$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$. Player 1 believes player 2 chooses $O$ with probability $q=0.3$. Which action maximizes her expected payoff, and what are the two expected payoffs?
options: $O$: $O$ yields $2$ and $F$ yields $1$
$O$: $O$ yields $1.4$ and $F$ yields $0.3$
$O$: $O$ yields $0.6$ and $F$ yields $0.3$
$F$: $O$ yields $0.6$ and $F$ yields $0.7$

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes, each player chooses $O$ or $F$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$. Mark player 1's best payoff in each column and player 2's best payoff in each row. Which profiles have both payoffs marked, that is, are pure Nash equilibria?
options: Only $(O,O)$
Only $(O,F)$
$(O,O)$ and $(F,F)$
No profile

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes, each player chooses $O$ or $F$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$. Starting from the equilibrium $(O,O)$, how much does each player's payoff change if she alone switches to $F$?
options: Player 1 loses $2$; player 2 loses $1$
Each player loses $1$
Player 1 loses $2$; player 2 gains $1$
Player 1 loses $1$; player 2 gains $1$

questions.question: In a variant of Battle of the Sexes player 1 enjoys going to $O$ alone: payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) are $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(1.5,0)$, $(F,O)=(0,0)$. What are the pure Nash equilibria?
options: None, since going alone breaks the coordination structure
Only $(O,O)$, since $O$ is now strictly dominant for player 1
$(O,O)$ and $(F,F)$, exactly as in the original game
$(O,O)$ and $(O,F)$, since player 1 now always chooses $O$

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes two players each choose $O$ or $F$; both want to choose the same option, but player 1 prefers that they meet at $O$ and player 2 at $F$. How does player 1 rank the outcomes?
options: Meeting at $O$, then either mismatch, then meeting at $F$
Meeting at $O$, then meeting at $F$, then either mismatch
Meeting at $F$, then meeting at $O$, then either mismatch
Meeting at $O$ and meeting at $F$ tied, then either mismatch

questions.question: Compare Battle of the Sexes (payoffs $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, mismatches $(0,0)$) with a Prisoner's Dilemma, in which each player has an action that is strictly better whatever the other does. Which contrast between their pure Nash equilibria is correct?
options: Sexes: dominant actions favouring different matches; Dilemma: one dominant action
Sexes: two efficient pure equilibria with a selection issue; Dilemma: one inefficient pure equilibrium
Sexes: two inefficient equilibria; Dilemma: a single inefficient equilibrium
Sexes: a single efficient equilibrium; Dilemma: a single inefficient equilibrium

questions.question: Change Battle of the Sexes so that both players prefer meeting at $O$: payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ are $(O,O)=(2,2)$, $(F,F)=(1,1)$, mismatches $(0,0)$. Which statement about the pure Nash equilibria of the new game is correct?
options: $(F,F)$ is no longer an equilibrium, since both players prefer $(O,O)$
$O$ becomes strictly dominant for both, so $(O,O)$ is the only one
Both $(O,O)$ and $(F,F)$ remain, but now $(O,O)$ Pareto dominates $(F,F)$
Nothing changes: the two equilibria still cannot be Pareto ranked

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes, each player chooses $O$ or $F$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$. Before playing, the players agree to meet at $F$; nothing enforces the agreement, and player 1 would rather meet at $O$. Which statement explains why each player keeps the agreement if she expects the other to keep it?
options: $(F,F)$ is a Nash equilibrium: expecting $F$, breaking the agreement alone pays $0$
The agreement changes the payoffs, so $F$ becomes strictly dominant for both players
The talk gives each player information about the payoffs that she did not have before
$(F,F)$ has the largest total payoff, so rational players do not move away from it

questions.question: Player 2's payoff at $(O,O)$ in Battle of the Sexes is changed to $a>0$: payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ are $(O,O)=(2,a)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, mismatches $(0,0)$. A profile Pareto dominates another if it is at least as good for both and strictly better for one. When does $(O,O)$ Pareto dominate $(F,F)$?
options: Exactly when $a>2$
Exactly when $a>1$
Exactly when $a\ge2$
For no value $a>0$

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes, each player chooses $O$ or $F$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$. At the mismatch $(O,F)$ each player plays a best response to some belief: player 1 to the belief that player 2 plays $O$, player 2 to the belief that player 1 plays $F$. Why is $(O,F)$ still not a Nash equilibrium?
options: $(O,F)$ is Pareto dominated, and a Pareto-dominated profile is never a Nash equilibrium
Beliefs must also be correct: against the actual $F$, player 1 should play $F$
Only player 1 is at fault: player 2's $F$ is a best response to player 1's actual $O$
Choosing one's own favourite option is never a best response in Battle of the Sexes

questions.question: In Battle of the Sexes, each player chooses $O$ or $F$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ (player 1's action first) $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$. Player 1's payoffs are replaced by $2^{v_1}$ (so $4$, $2$ and $1$), player 2's are kept. Which statement about the new game is correct, where player 1 believes player 2 chooses $O$ with probability $q$?
options: Same pure equilibria; player 1 prefers $O$ iff $q>\tfrac{1}{3}$
Only $(O,O)$ remains; player 1 prefers $O$ iff $q>\tfrac{1}{4}$
Only $(O,O)$ remains; player 1 prefers $O$ iff $q>\tfrac{1}{3}$
Same pure equilibria; player 1 prefers $O$ iff $q>\tfrac{1}{4}$

questions.question: Player 1 in Battle of the Sexes gets a third action $H$ (stay home): payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ are $(O,O)=(2,1)$, $(F,F)=(1,2)$, $(O,F)=(F,O)=(0,0)$, and $(H,O)=(H,F)=(0.5,0)$. Which statement about $H$ is correct?
options: $H$ is player 1's best response to $F$, since its payoff $0.5$ exceeds the mismatch payoff $0$
$H$ is strictly dominated by $O$, so elimination of dominated strategies removes it at once
No single pure strategy beats $H$ in both columns, yet $H$ is in no pure Nash equilibrium
$(H,O)$ and $(H,F)$ are Nash equilibria, since player 2 then gets $0$ whatever she does
